studyDesign: KEY POINT: this is a national emissions-inventory study (modelled), not a measurement-of-exposure study, and it contains NO table of per-vehicle-km emission factors. The only printed table is Table 1 (vehicle fleet counts, p.4). Fig 1 (p.3) ends in a box 'Emission Factor from Different Types of Vehicles (mg/km)' but the values are never printed; only rank orderings (abstract p.1, Conclusions p.18) are given. Questions 2, 3 and 5 therefore cannot be answered with numbers. What it gives: annual emissions (tons/yr; kg/yr for BaP) by broad class for 2013, 2016, 2019 and 2021, bar charts by emission-standard phase (Figs 3-5, 8-10), regional shares and gridded maps (Figs 6, 11). Method (Sec 2, pp.2-5): emissions = emission factor x activity (vehicle-km travelled, VKT). Activity follows the TEDS 11.0 (Taiwan Emission Data System v11.0) manual via a fuel-consumption method using fleet numbers (Table 1), average annual mileage, fuel efficiency and fuel sales by county/city (p.3); traffic-volume surveys by MOTC and local governments are used to spread mileage spatially (p.5). Emission-factor sources per Fig 1 (p.3) and Sec 2.3 (p.5): US EPA MOVES for PM2.5 (all vehicles; brake-wear PM2.5 also MOVES, tyre wear from TEDS) and for BaP (Fig 1: gasoline and diesel vehicles); MOBILE6.2 for NOx (all vehicles), diesel HC/benzene/formaldehyde, and HC and benzene evaporation for motorcycles and gasoline cars; chassis-dynamometer data for exhaust benzene and formaldehyde (motorcycles and gasoline passenger cars) and gasoline-vehicle HC ('data from the previous year's dynamometer measurements', times a measured 'fingerprint ratio'). Sec 2.4 also says emission factors 'are determined by Taiwan Emission Data system by TEPA'. Dynamometer methods (GC/MS purge-and-trap for benzene; Tedlar bag plus DNPH/HPLC for formaldehyde) are described briefly on p.3, citing [25]; no number of vehicles tested, cycle or conditions are given. BaP sampling (p.3) is described only for diesel PM [8]. Classes: self-use and business gasoline passenger cars, light-duty gasoline vehicles, four-stroke, two-stroke and electric motorcycles; diesel passenger cars, light-duty diesel, tourist buses, buses, self-use and business heavy-duty diesel trucks; electric categories; specially constructed vehicles; emission-standard phases I-VII. 'Motorcycle' is the paper's word; it never says 'scooter' and never says whether motorcycles are scooters. Pollutants: PM2.5, NOx, HC (criteria); benzene, formaldehyde, BaP (hazardous). Place: Taiwan, national and four regions (north, central, south, east) plus gridded maps (cell size not stated); no city or street results. Not covered: CO, SOx, PM10, toluene, xylenes, ethylbenzene, 1,3-butadiene, acetaldehyde (1,3-butadiene and acetaldehyde appear only in background text, pp.2-3, 12), metals, per-passenger-km, per-person, idle, cold start, concentrations, personal exposure, health outcomes. No statistical tests or confidence intervals; the only uncertainty figure is a cited 30% for fuel-based CO, NOx and NMHC factors in California (p.2).

findings.claim: The paper does not print per-vehicle-km emission factors for any pollutant or vehicle class; it gives only rank orderings of factors and annual national totals.
findings.value: No emission-factor values anywhere; Figure 1 box is only labelled 'Emission Factor from Different Types of Vehicles (mg/km)'
findings.quote: Fig 1 bottom box: 'Emission Factor from Different Types of Vehicles (mg/km)'; abstract and Conclusions give orderings only
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Text search of the full text finds no g/km or mg/km values for any vehicle class in this paper (the only g/km figures, p.2, are quoted from Zhang et al. [13] for Hangzhou passenger vehicles). CO, SOx, PM10 are not studied. Anyone needing per-km values must go to the cited sources, not this paper.
findings.useOnSite: This paper reports annual national emissions and rank orders of emission factors, not per-kilometre values.
findings.checkerNote: Claim confirmed by reading Fig 1 on the PDF page and grepping the text. Corrected the 'kind' label: it is an absence of data, not an author opinion.

findings.claim: Authors state the per-vehicle emission-factor ranking is motorcycle > gasoline >= diesel for benzene, and diesel > motorcycle >= gasoline for formaldehyde.
findings.value: Benzene factor order: motorcycle > gasoline >= diesel; formaldehyde: diesel > motorcycle >= gasoline (no magnitudes)
findings.quote: 'the emission sequence for benzene was motorcycle > gasoline ≥ diesel; the formaldehyde emission sequence was diesel > motorcycle ≥ gasoline' (abstract); same order p.18
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Per Fig 1 (p.3), exhaust benzene and formaldehyde for motorcycles and gasoline passenger cars come from chassis-dynamometer data; diesel benzene/formaldehyde and all evaporative benzene come from MOBILE6.2. Number of vehicles tested, cycle and conditions are not given (cites ref [25]). 'Gasoline' presumably means gasoline cars/light-duty vehicles. The orderings are stated, never tabulated, and the year or fleet they refer to is not stated.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwan's inventory ranks per-kilometre benzene emission factors highest for motorcycles, above gasoline vehicles and diesel (the paper prints the ordering, not the values).
findings.checkerNote: Quote located in abstract (p.1) and Conclusions (p.18). See the added finding on whether the ordering can be squared with the 2021 totals.

findings.claim: Authors state PM2.5 and NOx emission factors rank diesel > gasoline > motorcycle, and the HC factor ranks motorcycle > gasoline vehicles.
findings.value: PM2.5: diesel > gasoline > motorcycle (MOVES); NOx: diesel > gasoline > motorcycle (MOBILE6.2); HC: motorcycle > gasoline (dynamometer-compiled)
findings.quote: 'the emission sequence was diesel > gasoline > motorcycle ... the HC emission factor ... showed that motorcycle > gasoline vehicles' (abstract)
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: PM2.5 factor includes tyre and brake wear (p.6: 'PM2.5 emission includes tire and wear emission'). Body text (p.6) restates only gasoline vs diesel for PM2.5 and NOx, not motorcycle vs gasoline. For gasoline vehicles HC includes evaporative (vapour) emissions (p.10), so the abstract's HC ordering may mix exhaust and evaporative; the paper does not say.
findings.useOnSite: Per kilometre, the inventory puts motorcycle PM2.5 below gasoline cars but motorcycle hydrocarbons above them (ordering only).
findings.checkerNote: Abstract wording matches. Added the evaporative caveat for HC (p.10) and the clarification that p.6 only compares gasoline with diesel.

findings.claim: Total road vehicle-km travelled in Taiwan was about 148-159 billion km/yr, with gasoline passenger cars the largest share and four-stroke motorcycles second.
findings.value: 148 x10^9, 156 x10^9, 159 x10^9, 155 x10^9 km/yr in 2013, 2016, 2019, 2021; gasoline passenger cars 42.6%, four-stroke motorcycles 32.6%
findings.quote: '148 × 10^9, 156 × 10^9, 159 × 10^9, and 155 × 10^9 km/year in 2013, 2016, 2019, and 2021 ... gasoline passenger cars (42.6%), followed by four-stroke motorcycles (32.6%)'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Abstract does not say which year the 42.6% and 32.6% shares apply to; no table of VKT by class in the body. Sec 4 (p.18) gives only a ranking: gasoline cars > four-stroke motorcycles > light-duty diesel > heavy-duty diesel > diesel passenger cars > light-duty gasoline > commercial gasoline passenger cars > two-stroke motorcycles > diesel bus > public bus > special vehicles. VKT is estimated by a fuel-consumption method from fleet counts, average mileage, fuel efficiency and fuel sales (p.3), including freeways and all road types, not counted at street level.
findings.useOnSite: Four-stroke motorcycles account for about a third of vehicle-km on Taiwan's roads, second only to gasoline cars (abstract; year of share not stated).
findings.checkerNote: Abstract numbers and Sec 4 ranking match.

findings.claim: Table 1 lists about 13.6 million motorcycles in Taiwan in 2021 and about 544 thousand electric motorcycles, up from 38 thousand in 2013.
findings.value: Motorcycle 14,157 (2013), 13,643 (2021); Electric motorcycle 38 (2013), 544 (2021); table note: numerical value x10^3
findings.quote: Table 1 row 2021: Motorcycle 13,643; Electric 544. Row 2013: 14,157; 38. Note: '* numerical value × 10^3' (asterisk sits on the first cell, 5903)
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: The x10^3 multiplier is attached by asterisk to one cell only, so thousands for the rest of the table is inferred (consistent with the first cell). Source of counts not given; two-stroke and four-stroke not separated in the table; the table does not say whether 'Motorcycle' includes scooters. 544 is about 3.8% of Motorcycle + Electric in 2021, and 14.3 times the 2013 value (checker arithmetic from printed numbers). Table 1 also shows electric passenger cars rising from 0.4 to 144.4 (x10^3) 2013-2021.
findings.useOnSite: Taiwan's registered fleet in the paper's Table 1 is about 13.6 million motorcycles plus about 0.54 million electric motorcycles in 2021.
findings.checkerNote: Table read on the PDF page (p.4). Values and note exactly as the reader gave them.

findings.claim: Annual hydrocarbon emissions from motorcycles fell from 68,000 to 37,000 tons between 2013 and 2021, while gasoline vehicles (cars and light-duty) rose from 23,000 to 39,000 tons.
findings.quote: 'total HC emissions from motorcycles were 68,000, 48,000, 38,000, and 37,000 tons ... gasoline vehicles were 23,000, 30,000, 40,000, and 39,000 tons ... diesel vehicles were 8073, 9881, 9438, and 9211 tons'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: 'HC' is total hydrocarbons, not VOC or NMHC, and for gasoline vehicles includes evaporative emissions (p.10: 'not only from exhaust emissions but also from vaporization emissions'); Fig 1 shows MOBILE6.2 evaporative HC also applied to motorcycles. By 2019 and 2021 gasoline vehicles (40,000 and 39,000) are slightly above motorcycles (38,000 and 37,000), at odds with the Conclusions' 'Most hydrocarbon emissions were from motorcycles' (p.18). Totals match Fig 2c bar heights.
findings.useOnSite: In Taiwan's 2021 inventory, motorcycles emitted about 37,000 tons of hydrocarbons, a little under gasoline cars and light vehicles (39,000 t), having fallen about 46% from 2013 as two-stroke machines left the fleet (the 46% is the checker's ratio of the printed totals).
findings.checkerNote: All twelve numbers match the text; Fig 2c checked visually (2013 total about 100,000 t, 2021 about 85,000 t).

findings.claim: The paper says a larger proportion of gasoline-vehicle hydrocarbon emissions is vapour (evaporative) than for motorcycles.
findings.value: Qualitative; no percentages
findings.quote: 'Unlike motorcycles, a larger proportion of the HC emissions come from vapor emissions for gasoline vehicles.'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: No exhaust/evaporative split is quantified for any class. Evaporative HC and benzene for both motorcycles and gasoline cars are modelled with MOBILE6.2 (Fig 1, p.3; p.5), so motorcycle HC in the totals also includes a modelled evaporative part. The sentence compares proportions only; it does not state that motorcycle HC is mostly tailpipe.
findings.useOnSite: The paper says a larger fraction of gasoline-car hydrocarbons than of motorcycle hydrocarbons is evaporative; it does not quantify either.
findings.checkerNote: Quote exact. Softened the reader's inference that motorcycle HC is 'tailpipe-borne': the paper only says the evaporative share is smaller, and Fig 1 shows motorcycles also carry a modelled evaporative term.

findings.claim: Annual benzene emissions from motorcycles fell steeply, from 1,048 tons in 2013 to 286 tons in 2021; gasoline vehicles (cars and light-duty) emitted 721 tons in 2013 and 545 tons in 2021.
findings.quote: 'total benzene emissions from motorcycles were 1048, 571, 344, and 286 tons ... gasoline vehicles were 721, 721, 683, and 545 tons ... diesel vehicles were 95, 119, 115, and 113 tons'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Motorcycles were the largest benzene class only in 2013 (1,048 vs 721 t). From 2016 gasoline vehicles are larger (571 vs 721 t in 2016; 344 vs 683 in 2019; 286 vs 545 in 2021). Modelled inventory (dynamometer-based exhaust factors plus MOBILE6.2 evaporative), not ambient concentrations. Reading Fig 8a, the three gasoline vehicle bars (self-use car, business car, light-duty) add to roughly 640, 625, 585 and 495 t in 2013/2016/2019/2021, below the printed gasoline totals; the paper does not explain the gap (visual estimate).
findings.useOnSite: The inventory estimates motorcycle benzene at 1,048 t in 2013 but only 286 t in 2021; by 2021 gasoline cars and light vehicles (545 t) emitted about twice as much benzene in total.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers confirmed against the text and Fig 7a. Rewrote the reader's garbled caveat (it said 'exceeded ... in 2013 and 2016' then corrected itself) and added the Fig 8a sum gap.

findings.claim: The Conclusions say benzene was mainly emitted by gasoline vehicles, while the abstract and Conclusions also rank the motorcycle benzene factor highest; the paper does not reconcile the two.
findings.value: 2021 benzene totals: motorcycles 286 t vs gasoline vehicles 545 t; stated per-km factor order: motorcycle > gasoline
findings.quote: 'Benzene was mainly emitted by gasoline vehicles' (Sec 4); 'benzene emission factors had the following sequence: motorcycle > gasoline ≥ diesel' (Sec 4)
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: The reader suggested the two statements agree because cars travel more km. The paper does not show this. Its only VKT shares (abstract: gasoline passenger cars 42.6%, four-stroke motorcycles 32.6%, year not stated) differ about 1.3-fold, while 2021 benzene totals differ about 1.9-fold in gasoline's favour; but the gasoline total (545 t) includes light-duty vehicles whose VKT share is not printed. Using the cars-only bars of Fig 8a (about 330 t in 2021, visual) over 42.6% versus motorcycles 286 t over 32.6% gives similar per-km magnitudes, so a rough check is inconclusive and does not clearly support motorcycle > gasoline for 2021. The ordering may refer to another year or an older fleet; the paper does not say. Checker's rough arithmetic on printed and visually read numbers, offered only to show the ordering cannot be verified from this paper.
findings.useOnSite: Do not state a per-km motorcycle-over-car benzene ratio. The safe statement is that the paper says the motorcycle benzene factor ranks highest, without values or year.
findings.checkerNote: Quotes located (p.18). Replaced the reader's 'consistent only because cars travel more km' reconciliation, which the printed VKT shares do not establish.

findings.claim: Motorcycle formaldehyde emissions were small and falling (100 to 51 tons); diesel vehicles dominated (645 to 712 tons).
findings.quote: 'formaldehyde emissions from motorcycles was 100, 75, 59, and 51 tons ... gasoline vehicles were 140, 139, 125, and 98 tons ... diesel vehicles were 645, 780, 729, and 712 tons'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Figure 9 (p.14) reproduces the benzene panels of Figure 8 (axes 0-600 and 0-60 t, 'Phase' bars identical), so it cannot be used for formaldehyde by phase; captions say formaldehyde. Motorcycle share in 2021 is about 6% (51 of about 861 t; checker arithmetic from printed totals).
findings.useOnSite: Formaldehyde in the inventory is mainly a diesel issue; motorcycles contributed about 51 of roughly 860 tons in 2021 (checker's arithmetic from printed totals).
findings.checkerNote: Numbers match text; Fig 9 identical to Fig 8 confirmed on the PDF page; Fig 7b agrees with the totals.

findings.claim: BaP emissions from motorcycles are small (33 to 23 kg/yr) next to gasoline vehicles (191 to 140 kg) and diesel (390 to 189 kg).
findings.value: Motorcycles 33 / 28 / 25 / 23 kg; gasoline 191 / 191 / 169 / 140 kg; diesel 390 / 330 / 248 / 189 kg; diesel share 63% (2013) to 54% (2021)
findings.quote: 'total BaP emissions of motorcycles were 33, 28, 25, and 23 kg ... gasoline vehicles were 191, 191, 169, and 140 kg per year ... diesel vehicles were 390, 330, 248, and 189 kg ... decreased from 63% ... to 54%'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: BaP is estimated with MOVES as a component of particulate matter (p.5); Fig 1 lists MOVES BaP for 'gasoline and diesel vehicles' and Sec 2.1.2 (p.3) describes BaP sampling only for diesel PM [8], so the basis of the motorcycle BaP figure is not described. The Introduction (p.2) cites others saying BaP comes from motorcycle PM; the paper's own motorcycle total is the smallest class. Units are kg per year (not tons).
findings.useOnSite: For benzo(a)pyrene the paper's inventory is dominated by diesel and gasoline cars; motorcycles are a minor share (23 of about 352 kg in 2021, checker's arithmetic).
findings.checkerNote: Numbers and 63%/54% quote verified. Added the Fig 1 and Sec 2.1.2 note on the basis for motorcycle BaP.

findings.claim: Motorcycle PM2.5 emissions (2,456 to 2,123 tons/yr) are smaller than gasoline-vehicle (4,295-4,844) or diesel (5,857 to 4,561) totals, and include tyre and brake wear.
findings.quote: 'total PM2.5 emissions from motorcycles were 2456, 2235, 2223, and 2123 tons ... gasoline vehicles were 4295, 4833, 4844, and 4444 tons ... diesel vehicles were 5857, 5634, 5088, and 4561 tons'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: 'PM2.5 emission includes tire and wear emission' (p.6), so not tailpipe-only. Motorcycle PM2.5 is about 19% of the 2021 three-class total (checker arithmetic). The totals support 'fumes more than dust' only as a rank relative to other vehicles; about 2,100 t/yr of motorcycle PM2.5 remains.
findings.useOnSite: Motorcycle PM2.5 in the inventory is lower than cars or diesel, and includes non-exhaust wear particles.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers verified on p.6.

findings.claim: The Conclusions give diesel vehicles 92.8% of mobile PM2.5, which does not agree with the printed totals in the Results.
findings.value: Conclusions: 'Diesel vehicles had the largest (92.8%) PM2.5 emissions'; Results totals imply diesel is about 41% of 2021 PM2.5 (checker arithmetic)
findings.quote: 'Diesel vehicles had the largest (92.8%) PM2.5 emissions for mobile sources.'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: 2021 totals: diesel 4,561, gasoline 4,444, motorcycle 2,123 t, so diesel is about 41%. p.6 itself says diesel total is 'slightly higher than that of gasoline vehicles'. The 92.8% cannot be reconciled; it may refer to something else (for example PM from exhaust only), but the paper does not say.
findings.useOnSite: Do not use the 92.8% figure.
findings.checkerNote: Quote located; arithmetic 4561/(4561+4444+2123)=41.0%.

findings.claim: Motorcycle NOx (about 6,000 t/yr) is small compared with diesel (250,000-290,000 t/yr).
findings.quote: 'total NOx emissions of motorcycles ... 6398, 6501, 6024, and 6111 tons ... gasoline vehicles were 13,484, 15,054, 15,116, and 14,110 tons ... diesel vehicles were 260,000, 290,000, 260,000, and 250,000 tons'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Context only; not a hydrocarbon or street-fume metric. Diesel figures are rounded to two significant figures in the text.
findings.useOnSite: Diesel dominates NOx in Taiwan's inventory; motorcycles are a minor contributor.
findings.checkerNote: Numbers verified.

findings.claim: Two-stroke motorcycles were phased out of production in 2004 and were about 2% of vehicles in 2021 (453,675 units), contributing under 0.5% of PM.
findings.value: 453,675 two-stroke motorcycles in 2021, 'approximately 2% of total vehicles'; 'less than 0.5% for PM'
findings.quote: 'two-stroke motorcycles were phased out of their production in 2004 because of their higher pollution ... 453,675, which was approximately 2% of total vehicles in Taiwan in 2021 ... less than 0.5% for PM'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: The 2% is of all vehicles in the paper's fleet (Table 1 sums to about 22.5 million incl. cars and trucks); relative to the 13.6 million motorcycles it is about 3.3% (checker arithmetic). The 0.5% applies to PM only; HC and benzene shares are not printed (see added finding for a visual estimate). Reason for the phase-out is given only as 'higher pollution'.
findings.useOnSite: Two-stroke motorcycles were phased out of production in 2004 and by 2021 were about 2% of all vehicles (about 3% of motorcycles).
findings.checkerNote: Quote located. Added the denominator clarification.

findings.claim: The authors attribute the large fall in motorcycle hydrocarbon and benzene emissions to the phase-out of two-stroke machines and to tighter emission standards.
findings.value: Motorcycle HC 68,000 to 37,000 t; benzene 1,048 to 286 t (2013 to 2021)
findings.quote: 'The reduction of emissions from motorcycles was more obvious as a result of the phase-out of two-stroke motorcycles'; 'portion of benzene emissions gradually declined after 2016 due to the phase-out of two-stroke motorcycles'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Interpretation, not a separate analysis. The p.12 sentence 'Benzene emissions of two-stroke motorcycles were lower than those from four-stroke motorcycles by about 150 tons' does not state a year. Fig 8a (visual) shows four-stroke motorcycle benzene about 455 t (2013), 285 (2016), 250 (2019), 215 (2021). Against the motorcycle totals, two-stroke would be about 590 t in 2013 (higher than four-stroke) and about 70 t in 2021 (lower by about 145 t), so the 150-t sentence fits 2021 but not 2013. The text also says motorcycle 'main source of HC came from four-stroke motorcycles in 2008 and 2010' (p.9), years outside the study.
findings.useOnSite: The authors credit the retirement of two-stroke motorcycles and stricter standards for the fall in motorcycle HC and benzene.
findings.checkerNote: Quotes exact. The reader said the 150-t sentence 'cannot be matched' to Fig 8a; it can for 2021 (not 2013). Caveat rewritten.

findings.claim: Newer emission-standard phases emit less per vehicle, so fleet age drives the totals; by 2021 four-stroke motorcycle emissions were mostly phase V and VI.
findings.value: Four-stroke motorcycle benzene largest phase: III in 2013, V in 2016, 2019 and 2021; BaP phase VI share 51% in 2021
findings.quote: 'four-stroke motorcycles with phase III, V, V, and V vehicles had the largest portion of emissions in the years 2013, 2016, 2019, and 2021'; 'In the year 2021, the number of phase VI vehicles increased, which caused the emission percentage to reach 51%.'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Phases are Taiwan's successive standards and are not defined in this paper. Average fleet age not given. For gasoline cars the largest benzene phase is still phase III in all four years (p.13). Fig 1 lists MOBILE6.2 inputs 'Zero mileage emission rate', 'Deterioration rate', 'Cumulative mileage', so mileage deterioration is a model input.
findings.useOnSite: Within the inventory, newer-standard motorcycles emit less per vehicle, and old gasoline cars (phase III) remain the biggest benzene source among cars.
findings.checkerNote: Quotes located; Fig 8a bars agree (2013 largest segment Phase III, later V).

findings.claim: The authors attribute rising gasoline-vehicle HC in 2016 and 2019 to emission deterioration with mileage and exhaust-control degradation after warranty.
findings.value: Gasoline vehicle HC 23,000 to 40,000 t (2013 to 2019)
findings.quote: 'The deterioration of emissions caused by the increase in vehicle mileage and the inefficiency of the exhaust control equipment after the warranty led to the increase in gasoline vehicle emissions in 2016 and 2019.'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Stated explanation only; no analysis of mileage effects shown, none for motorcycles.
findings.useOnSite: The paper says emissions deteriorate as vehicles accumulate mileage (explanation, not a tested result).
findings.checkerNote: Quote exact.

findings.claim: Hydrocarbon and benzene emissions are concentrated in the populous north, central and south of western Taiwan; the east contributes about 2.6-2.9%.
findings.quote: 'regional portions were at 34.5, 35.7, 37.1, and 36.9%' (HC, north); benzene north '651, 503, 419, and 341 tons'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Regions plus gridded maps only; grid-cell size is not stated, so legend values (HC >22.2 ton/yr, benzene >0.43 ton/yr) are per unspecified cell. Maps show high cells along the western plain, the north and along road corridors; no city or street resolution. In the HC paragraph the tonnages '37,000, 31,000, 29,000, and 28,000' follow the east's 2.6% but are the southern totals (37.3% of the roughly 99,000 t national total in 2013 is about 37,000); the sentence is garbled. Central HC not given. Text refers to benzene 'in 2002' (p.16) and motorcycle HC 'in 2008 and 2010' (p.9), outside the study years. Authors link the pattern to 'Population distribution and human activity' (p.12).
findings.useOnSite: Hydrocarbon and benzene emissions are highest in the north, central and south regions where people and traffic are concentrated; the paper does not resolve city centres.
findings.checkerNote: Percentages and benzene tonnages cross-check against class totals (e.g. 651/1,864 = 34.9%). Corrected the reader's reading of the garbled paragraph and the 'per grid cell' wording.

findings.claim: The authors state mobile sources are important air pollution sources affecting health, especially in urban areas, citing a TEPA handbook for the national share.
findings.value: Mobile sources about 30% of PM2.5, 50% of NOx, 19% of hydrocarbon emissions in Taiwan
findings.quote: 'In Taiwan, the mobile sources contributed approximately 30% of PM2.5, 50% of NOx, and 19% of hydrocarbon emission [26]; therefore, the mobile sources can be considered the important air pollution sources and they affect the human health, especially in urban areas.'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Cited from TEPA Handbook [26] (in Chinese), year not given. The health clause is an assertion without epidemiological reference. The paper measures no concentration or exposure.
findings.useOnSite: The paper (citing TEPA) puts mobile sources at about 19% of Taiwan's hydrocarbon emissions, 30% of PM2.5 and 50% of NOx.
findings.checkerNote: Quote located on p.6.

findings.claim: The Introduction cites IARC for benzene as a known carcinogen and formaldehyde and BaP as probable carcinogens, and says benzene is the main hazardous air pollutant in gasoline-vehicle exhaust.
findings.value: Benzene: 'known carcinogen'; formaldehyde and BaP: 'probable carcinogens' (as worded in the paper)
findings.quote: 'benzene as a known carcinogen, and formaldehyde and BaP ... as probable carcinogens [16]. ... benzene is the main hazardous air pollutant in the exhaust of gasoline vehicles'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Ref [16] as listed is IARC Monographs vol. 92 (2010) 'Some non-heterocyclic polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and some related exposures', a volume titled for PAHs, so the benzene and formaldehyde attributions rest on that single citation. The paper gives no classification groups. Cite IARC directly. No dose-response or risk figures appear.
findings.useOnSite: Cite IARC directly for classifications; this paper only repeats them in its introduction.
findings.checkerNote: Quote located; added the reference-title observation.

findings.claim: The Introduction (citing others) says benzene is emitted mainly by motorcycles and gasoline vehicles, and BaP mainly from particulate matter from motorcycles and diesel.
findings.value: Qualitative
findings.quote: 'Benzene is mainly emitted by motorcycles and gasoline vehicles [17,18]. ... BaP mainly comes from the particulate matter emitted by motorcycles [21] and diesel vehicles [22].'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: Cited statements, not this study's results; the paper's own BaP results show motorcycles as the smallest class (23 kg vs 140 and 189 kg in 2021). findings.value: Qualitative recommendation
findings.quote: 'the stringent emission standards and the retirement of older vehicles can be more effective in the reduction of airborne pollutant emissions ... the cleaner vehicles application can reduce the airborne pollutant emissions and eliminate the exposure and health risk.'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: 'Cleaner vehicles' is not defined as electric. No electrification scenario is modelled; the exposure and health-risk claim is asserted, not tested. 'Electric' appears only in Table 1, chart legends, the sentence on p.7 that phase V and VI and electric motorcycles replaced phase III and IV motorcycles, and a passing mention of 'the widespread use of electric vehicles' (p.1).

findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)

The motorcycle panel is labelled 'Four-stroke motorcycle' and appears to hold the electric motorcycle segment, which the paper never explains. Electric motorcycles are about 3.8% of the Table 1 motorcycle count, so a roughly 5% share of motorcycle PM2.5 would mean per-vehicle wear PM comparable to gasoline motorcycles; this is the checker's inference and is uncertain. The paper does not state electric-vehicle PM2.5 factors. A red Electric segment is not visible in the NOx or HC bars (Figs 4a, 5a) or the benzene bars (Fig 8a) at the PDF's resolution, but the paper does not say electric vehicles emit no HC or benzene; this is not stated.

This complicates a claim that electrification removes all particle emissions.

findings.claim: The Conclusions state most hydrocarbon emissions were from motorcycles, but the Results' own totals show this was true in 2013 and 2016 only.
findings.quote: 'Most hydrocarbon emissions were from motorcycles, followed by gasoline and diesel vehicles.'
findings.significance: n/a (no statistical tests or confidence intervals in the paper)
findings.caveats: The sentence is undated. Motorcycles were also the largest class in 2013 and 2016 only (from the printed totals); in 2019 and 2021 gasoline vehicles are slightly larger. Motorcycles were 43% of 2021 HC (37,000 of about 85,000 t, checker arithmetic).
findings.useOnSite: Say motorcycles were the largest hydrocarbon class in 2013 and 2016 and about on par with gasoline vehicles in 2019-2021.
findings.checkerNote: Added by checker from the Conclusions (p.18) against the Results.

limitations: No limitations section. No uncertainty ranges or sensitivity analysis for any estimate; the only uncertainty figure is a cited 30% for fuel-based CO, NOx and NMHC factors in California (p.2).

Emission factors rely on US models (MOVES, MOBILE6.2) and on dynamometer data described only by reference to an earlier paper [25]; number of vehicles tested, cycles and mileage are not given (pp.3, 5). Motorcycle BaP basis is not described.
VKT is estimated from fuel sales, fleet counts and averages, not traffic counts (p.3). The abstract's VKT class shares carry no year.
Results are annual national and regional totals with gridded maps of unstated cell size; no street-level, city-centre, idle, cold-start or traffic-light results.
Evaporative emissions are modelled (MOBILE6.2) and folded into the HC and benzene totals; they are not separated in the printed numbers.
Only four years (2013, 2016, 2019, 2021) are reported, so trends rest on four points.
No concentration, exposure or epidemiological data; health statements are citations or assertions.

Editing errors reduce reliability: Fig 9 duplicates Fig 8; text refers to years outside the study (benzene 'in 2002' p.16; HC 'in 2008 and 2010' p.9); in the formaldehyde regional paragraph (p.18) the southern line prints percentages where tonnages belong and the 2021 northern tonnage (327 t) conflicts with its 30.4% share (about 262 t of the roughly 861 t total); the regional HC paragraph (p.12) is garbled; the Conclusions' 92.8% diesel PM2.5 share conflicts with the Results; Fig 8a bars for gasoline vehicles sum to less than the printed totals (visual estimate); the 'Electirc' legend typo.
complications: No emission-factor table exists, so the site cannot cite per-km values for any pollutant or class from this paper. CO, SOx, PM10, toluene, xylenes, ethylbenzene, 1,3-butadiene, acetaldehyde, metals and PAHs other than BaP are not reported.

The motorcycle-to-gasoline-car ratio per pollutant cannot be computed because no factors are printed. Labelled note: the paper states only that motorcycle factors rank above gasoline for benzene and HC, below for PM2.5 and NOx, and at or above for formaldehyde.

By 2021 motorcycle benzene (286 t) is about half of gasoline-vehicle benzene (545 t), and motorcycle HC (37,000 t) is slightly below gasoline-vehicle HC (39,000 t). 'Scooters are the main hydrocarbon or benzene source' was true in 2013 (and for HC also 2016) but not in the 2021 totals.

The Conclusions say 'Benzene was mainly emitted by gasoline vehicles' and 'Most hydrocarbon emissions were from motorcycles', each in tension with the paper's own totals or its factor ordering; the paper never reconciles per-km factor order with totals, and the abstract's VKT shares (year unstated) do not settle it.

Motorcycle benzene fell about 73% and HC about 46% in eight years (from printed totals), credited to retiring two-stroke machines and tighter standards. The problem the site describes is shrinking in the inventory and today's fleet is mostly four-stroke phase V/VI. Figures imply the remaining two-stroke machines still contribute disproportionately (visual estimate).

Motorcycle PM2.5 is a minor share and includes wear; motorcycle BaP is the smallest class (23 kg vs 189 kg diesel, 2021). This supports 'fumes more than dust' only relative to other vehicles; about 2,100 t/yr of motorcycle PM2.5 remains, and the paper's PM2.5 includes tyre and brake wear.

Electric motorcycles appear in the PM2.5 chart (Fig 3a) with a segment of roughly 100 t in 2021 (visual), so electrification does not remove particle emissions in this inventory; the paper does not explain or quantify it.
Motorcycle formaldehyde is small (51 t of about 861 t in 2021).
Totals are national emissions (tons emitted), not what a pedestrian breathes: no link to street-level concentration, no idle or red-light data, no child, elderly, rider or pedestrian information.
The paper models no electrification scenario and says nothing about electric motorcycle exhaust beyond fleet counts and chart legends.
The paper never says 'scooter', and Table 1 does not say whether 'Motorcycle' includes scooters or gasoline-only; the 13.6 million count x10^3 multiplier is inferred from one asterisk.

Leads in this paper's reference list (not read): ref [18] Tsai, Huang and Chiang 2014, Atmos. Environ. 99, 215-226 (VOCs in motorcycle exhaust, real-world driving) and ref [25] Tsai et al. 2018, Aerosol Air Qual. Res. 18, 3056-3067 (fuel economy and VOC exhaust of motorcycles by mileage) are the likely sources of the dynamometer data and may hold per-km motorcycle numbers.
correctionsToAbstractLevelNotes: The abstract-level note that motorcycles have the lowest PM2.5 per vehicle-km but higher hydrocarbons and benzene than gasoline cars is supported only as a rank ordering (abstract p.1; Sec 4 p.18). No per-km numbers exist in the paper, and the benzene ordering is hard to square with the 2021 totals.
PM2.5 factors include tyre and brake wear, so the 'low PM2.5' result is not purely exhaust, and electric motorcycles appear in the PM2.5 chart.
Benzene totals: motorcycles exceeded gasoline vehicles only in 2013 (1,048 vs 721 t); gasoline vehicles were larger in 2016, 2019, 2021 (721 vs 571; 683 vs 344; 545 vs 286).
HC totals: motorcycles larger only in 2013 and 2016; 2019 and 2021 gasoline vehicles slightly larger (40,000 vs 38,000; 39,000 vs 37,000), though the Conclusions say most HC came from motorcycles.
Motorcycle emissions fell steeply 2013 to 2021: benzene 1,048 to 286 t, HC 68,000 to 37,000 t, formaldehyde 100 to 51 t, BaP 33 to 23 kg, PM2.5 2,456 to 2,123 t, NOx roughly flat (6,398 to 6,111 t).
The 92.8% diesel PM2.5 share in the Conclusions is not supported by the Results' own totals.
The paper is national and regional; nothing on city centres, idling, cold starts or pedestrians, and no health outcomes are assessed.

answersToQuestions: 1. Inventory (modelled), not a new measurement campaign. Activity (VKT) follows the TEDS 11.0 manual via a fuel-consumption method (p.3); emission factors from MOVES (PM2.5, BaP), MOBILE6.2 (NOx, diesel HC/benzene/formaldehyde, all evaporative HC/benzene) and chassis-dynamometer data (exhaust benzene and formaldehyde for motorcycles and gasoline passenger cars; gasoline HC) (Fig 1 p.3; Sec 2.3 p.5). Years 2013, 2016, 2019, 2021 (fleet 2013-2021, Table 1 p.4). Classes: self-use and business gasoline cars, light-duty gasoline, four-stroke/two-stroke/electric motorcycles; diesel cars, light-duty, tourist buses, buses, heavy-duty trucks; electric categories; specially constructed vehicles; phases I-VII. The paper never says 'scooter'.

2. Not available. No per-km emission factors are printed. Only rank orders: PM2.5 diesel > gasoline > motorcycle; NOx diesel > gasoline > motorcycle; HC motorcycle > gasoline; benzene motorcycle > gasoline >= diesel; formaldehyde diesel > motorcycle >= gasoline (abstract p.1; Sec 4 p.18). CO, SOx, PM10 not studied; 'HC' is total hydrocarbons. Annual totals are in the chart-ready table.

3. Not available. Only benzene, formaldehyde and BaP are studied; toluene, xylenes, ethylbenzene, 1,3-butadiene, acetaldehyde, other PAHs and metals are not reported. Labelled ratio note: no motorcycle-to-gasoline-car ratio can be computed from printed numbers; the paper's ordering is motorcycle above gasoline for benzene, motorcycle >= gasoline for formaldehyde.

4. Annual totals by class are in the chart-ready Table A (pp.6-16). Printed shares: diesel BaP 63% (2013) to 54% (2021) (p.16); two-stroke under 0.5% of PM (p.6); VKT gasoline cars 42.6%, four-stroke motorcycles 32.6% (abstract, year not stated); mobile sources about 30% PM2.5, 50% NOx, 19% hydrocarbon of Taiwan's emissions (p.6, citing TEPA); diesel '92.8%' PM2.5 (p.18, conflicts with Results). Total VKT 148, 156, 159, 155 x10^9 km (p.1). VKT by class is not tabulated; Sec 4 (p.18) gives the ranking only.
5. Nothing per passenger-km or per person; only vehicle counts (Table 1) and VKT.

6. Two-stroke: production phased out 2004 'because of their higher pollution'; 453,675 units in 2021 (about 2% of all vehicles), under 0.5% of PM (p.6). Authors credit the two-stroke phase-out for the fall in motorcycle HC and benzene (pp.9, 16). No two-stroke factors are printed; the 'about 150 tons lower than four-stroke' benzene sentence (p.12) is undated and fits Fig 8a for 2021 but not 2013 (visual). Figures imply two-stroke was a large share of motorcycle HC and benzene in 2013 (see added finding). Fleet age: emissions split by standard phase; newer phases emit less; four-stroke motorcycle emissions mostly phase V/VI by 2019-2021 (p.12; BaP phase VI 51% in 2021, p.15); phase III gasoline cars remain the largest benzene/NOx source among cars (pp.8, 13); mileage deterioration is a model input (Fig 1) and the authors invoke it for gasoline HC (p.10). Average fleet age is not given. Trends 2013-2021: motorcycle benzene 1,048 to 286 t, HC 68,000 to 37,000 t, formaldehyde 100 to 51 t, BaP 33 to 23 kg, PM2.5 2,456 to 2,123 t, NOx about flat; gasoline vehicle HC rose 23,000 to 39,000 t and benzene fell 721 to 545 t.

7. Spatial: four regions plus gridded maps (cell size unstated). HC north 34.5-37.1%, south 33.0-37.3%, east 2.6%; benzene north 34.9-36.7%, south 32.2-36.0%, east about 2.9% (pp.12, 16). Emissions follow population and human activity (p.12; Conclusions: 'dominant in western Taiwan'). No cities or urban cores, no street level. Idle and cold start: not addressed. Evaporative: HC and benzene evaporation modelled with MOBILE6.2 for motorcycles and gasoline cars (Fig 1; p.5); 'a larger proportion of the HC emissions come from vapor emissions for gasoline vehicles' than for motorcycles (p.10); not quantified.

8. Conclusions (pp.18-19): 'the stringent emission standards and the retirement of older vehicles can be more effective in the reduction of airborne pollutant emissions. In urban areas, the mobile emission is relatively important; therefore, the cleaner vehicles application can reduce the airborne pollutant emissions and eliminate the exposure and health risk.' Also 'Our results showed that the stringent emission standards have the effect of reducing the HC exhaust emissions of gasoline and diesel vehicles' (p.18). 'Most hydrocarbon emissions were from motorcycles' and 'Benzene was mainly emitted by gasoline vehicles' (p.18). No explicit recommendation to electrify motorcycles; 'electric' appears only in fleet counts, chart legends, the p.7 replacement sentence, and a passing mention on p.1.
